raw_response:
I have been farming this land in Quzhou for nearly thirty years. The soil here on the North China Plain is flat and fertile, and we have reliable well water for irrigation. I see no reason to change what has always worked. This year, I will plant my entire 8 mu to the winter wheat–summer maize double-cropping rotation. Everyone in the village does this; the grain station guarantees a minimum price for wheat, and there is always a buyer for maize. I will not plant cotton—too much hand labor, too many sprays, and the market price jumps around too much for my taste.

For the wheat, I will buy improved Jimai variety seeds from the township supply store. After the maize harvest, I will run the rotary tiller to chop the stubble and level the seedbed. I will spread basal compound fertilizer before sowing in early October, then topdress urea at the jointing stage in spring. Wheat needs water at the critical times, so I will irrigate four times: once before winter to help the seedlings harden, once at green-up, once at jointing, and once at grain filling. I will also keep the sprays regular—one herbicide application early on, plus insecticide for aphids and fungicide for rust, about four sprayings in total. I expect around 500 kg per mu if the weather cooperates.

For the maize, I will buy hybrid seeds—Denghai or Nongda, whichever the dealer recommends this year. Time is short between wheat harvest and the summer rains, so I will not till. I will direct-seed the maize straight into the wheat stubble the same day the wheat comes off. Maize needs two irrigations here, one at the jointing–booting stage and one during grain filling. I will side-dress fertilizer at sowing and again when the plants are knee-high. Three sprayings will be enough: one herbicide and two insecticides for corn borer. I expect about 550 kg per mu.

This plan keeps my labor manageable, my costs predictable, and my grain secure.
